newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Europe rain not enough, dry weather to return.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Europe rain not enough, dry weather to return.

text.p: After a wet weekend and a rainy start to the week the dry conditions which have dominated Europe's weather for months were set to return from Wednesday onwards.
Farmers welcomed the recent rain, but they still have long term fears. And domestic water suppliers said it had done nothing to improve the long term outlook.
The latest analysis from Portugal, where drought has destroyed 50 to 70 per cent of winter cereals crops, has driven home the scale of Europe's water problem.
France is launching a nationwide debate on how to make controls on water use fairer and more effective. A stream of local authorities have slapped controls on irrigation.
Rain fell over much of northeastern France again on Tuesday, but forecasters predicted dry, sunny weather would return on Wednesday.
The clear weather was likely to persist through to Saturday, Meteo France forecaster Dominique Escale said.
A string of rainy days has given crops a good watering but has not been heavy enough to replenish depleted water tables, Escale said.
"The rain has brought a bit of relief to the countryside, decreasing the risk of forest fires, but it has not been enough" to end the dry spell, she said.
Scattered rains fell in eastern farming areas of the UK on Monday and overnight, but their impact on parched crops will be small, farming and weather analysts said on Tuesday.
"It's not enough to break any drought," a spokesman for the London Weather Centre said.
"That's not going to do any good," was the response of one farming source in East Anglia to reported rain levels.

The weather has done nothing to improve the outlook for domestic supplies. A spokeswoman for Anglia Water, which supplies water to households in much of eastern England, said the rain had made "not a jot of difference."

The region is officially designated as semi-arid, she said. In normal times it gets half of the national average rainfall, but since April 1995 it has had just 75 per cent of its "normal" rain. Since the start of this year that has fallen to 40 percent, going down to 30 percent in April.
"We would need weeks of rain to make a dent in our situation," she said. "We're very happy to have it. We love it," she said, but the weekend rain was not enough.
Even so there were no restrictions on domestic water use in the area and none were planned. "We feel the resources in place should be enough to avoid restrictions," she said. "But never say never."
Farmers in the region, whose supply is regulated by the Environment Agency, are already limiting abstraction on a voluntary basis.

Recent rain has done little to help Spain's drought hit farmers, according to grain traders. "Rain was after all very limited," one Madrid based trader said. "A drought in Spain is very tough, more dangerous than in the northern countries because we've got the hottest weather."
They said the lack of rain was hurting the southern regions most.
In Italy, heavy weeked rainstorms throughout the north, have helped to lessen some of the effects of months of drought, the Central Office for Agrarian Ecology said.
An official of the Rome-based state monitoring agency said rainstorms were registered throughout the country from Rome northwards.
In Portugal, one of the worst winter droughts in the last 150 years has destroyed an estimated 50 to 70 percent of winter cereal crops, an Agriculture Ministry official said on Monday.

Deputy Secretary of State for Agriculture Carlos Cunha said that rain last week in Portugal's southern cereal-producing Alentejo region might save pasture but not winter cereal crops, predominantly wheat.
In 1996 Portugal produced around 415,000 tonnes of wheat, up from 360,000 tonnes the previous year.
Irrigated spring and summer cereals have not been affected by the drought because dams are full.

"Even if it rains from now until the end of May it won't save winter crops. It's too late," Cunha told Reuters. "There was no rain in February and March when it was needed and temperatures have been five degrees above average for this time of year."
The forecast for this week is for more dry weather and temperatures of around 25 degrees centigrade.
Cunha said the Portuguese government was considering whether to disburse money from the so-called "calamities fund" to help farmers in some parts of the Alentejo.
He said Portugal would ask the European Union for financial and technical help in tackling the effects of the drought.
